title: As the ends and ultimates of all things accord in some mean and measure with their inceptions and originals, that same multiplicit concordance which leads forth growth from birth accomplishing by a retrogressive metamorphosis that minishing and ablation towards the final which is agreeable unto nature so is it with our subsolar being.
html_source:
This difficult, but not insignificant, passage paraphrases Aristotle quoting Empedocles, who argues a cyclical theory of creation, in whose first stages love adjoins things in such an indiscriminate manner as to produce monstrous beasts such as the ox-man. These creatures, unable to reproduce, gradually disappear from the population, a manifestation of nature’s self-correcting tendencies.

Aristotle: “Thus in the original combinations the ‘ox-progeny’ if they failed to reach a determinate end must have arisen through the corruption of some principle corresponding to what is now the seed.” The corrupted principle stressed in the Oxen of the Sun chapter is that of man’s duty to “multiply and replenish the earth,” avoided by young Irishmen of the time.
